newsitem.title: USA: Billboard magazine recalculating way it ranks singles.
newsitem.headline: Billboard magazine recalculating way it ranks singles.

text.p: Billboard, the bible of the music industry, is changing the way it ranks its chart of the top 100 songs, a widely followed gauge of trends in the recording business.
"We're looking at ways to come up with a better formula to determine the most popular singles," said Geoff Mayfield, director of charts for Billboard magazine.
In addition to its role in the music industry, Billboard's Hot 100 chart has been cited by newspapers, radio stations and magazines as a barometer of American listening tastes for more than 50 years.
Topping this week's chart is singer Toni Braxton's "Un-break My Heart", distributed by Arista, a unit of Bertelsmann AG.

While the ranking system may be changing, getting to the top of the charts will be as important as ever to the world's six major labels as well as independent producers and artists. This is especially true now that the rapid growth of recent years is slowing in the $40 billion-a-year industry.
Mayfield said the magazine had been working on the new system for more than a year. It could be unveiled as early as January.

"Five years ago we began using radio information from Broadcast Data Systems and sales data from Soundscan to better measure the popularity of songs," he said. "The exercise we're going through now is to make sure the use of data best reflects each song's popularity."
Until the late 1980s, industry sales data were often manipulated by record companies and promoters who showered money and gifts on retailers and radio stations.

To get better sales readings, in 1991 Billboard began using data from SoundScan, a Hartsdale, N.Y.-based company that uses computer technology to track sales, and New York-based Broadcast Data Systems, which measures radio airplay via computer.

"Perception and reality used to be two different things in the record business. We're much closer than we were, thanks to Soundscan, but we still need to be more accurate and sophisticated," said Thomas White, a specialist in artists' rights.

The latest changes in the charts come amid concern about how pricing affects rankings. Some record companies have been offering singles to retailers at discount prices, encouraging faster sales, industry sources said.

"The practice of deep discounting singles by high-profile artists is certainly one of the issues that heightens the priority of examining our chart formula, but it is by no means the only issue we seek to address," Mayfield said.
He also said that changes in the radio industry, including a move to more specialized formats, may be taken into account.
"One of the things that we're weighing is whether it is appropriate to introduce other radio formats to that panel," he said.
With new technologies providing more accurate sales data, the record industry has gradually adopted a more corporate way of doing things, a trend many expect to continue.

"The record industry has always been based on 'feel'," said White, the artists' rights expert. "In large part, it has made a lot of decisions by the seat of its pants and that comes as a result of entrepreneurial spirit and views that growth was infinite.

"It's now possible through technology to track all types of entertainment and this comes at a time when the industry is slowing down and it becomes increasingly necessary to broaden the sample from which the data is taken," he said.
